title: PPO: Proximal Policy Optimization
hook: Reinforcement learning is notoriously unstable. PPO's fix is simple: never let a single update move the policy too far. That restraint made it the field's workhorse.
key_points: Limits how far each policy update can change behavior, keeping training stable.
Uses a clipped objective that's simple to implement yet effective.
Reaches strong results with first-order optimization and easy tuning.
Became the default RL method, including the RL step inside RLHF.
content_html: John Schulman and colleagues at OpenAI wanted the reliability of careful policy-gradient methods without their complexity. PPO's idea is to improve the policy with each update but stop it from changing too drastically in one step. It delivers stable, sample-efficient training with plain gradient descent and little tuning, which is why it spread across robotics, games, and later the RL step in RLHF.
extra_html:
How it works

Policy gradient methods can take a step so large it wrecks performance. PPO guards against this with a clipped surrogate objective: it measures the ratio between the new and old policy's probability for each action, and clips that ratio so updates favoring an action are capped once the policy has moved far enough. The result discourages overly aggressive changes while still letting the policy improve, all using standard first-order optimization instead of the heavier machinery earlier methods required.

Why it matters

Before PPO, getting reinforcement learning to train reliably often meant complex algorithms or fragile hyperparameters. PPO offered a rare combination of simplicity, stability, and strong results, so it became a default choice across the field. That reliability is exactly why it was picked as the optimizer for the reinforcement-learning stage of RLHF in systems like InstructGPT.
